title: Outage: a Python service's log is filling /var

lines.text: 14:00 monitoring: etl1 /var 97% full and rising; PostgreSQL's data is on /var
14:12 monitoring: etl1 /var 100%; PostgreSQL stopped (could not write to its log: No space left on device)

nodes.label: invsync
nodes.status: {rotationLive ? "Rotating at 50 MB, INFO" : loadedCode == "zero" ? "RotatingFileHandler, backupCount 0: never rolls over" : "FileHandler at DEBUG: grows forever"}

objective: Write logs to a file that rotates by size or time
secondaryObjectives: Configure logging once at startup with basicConfig or dictConfig, and use a named logger per module
Choose the level for each message, from DEBUG to CRITICAL

sources.cite: logging.handlers: RotatingFileHandler and WatchedFileHandler, Python 3.15 documentation (docs.python.org)
sources.note: Relevant text: RotatingFileHandler(filename, mode='a', maxBytes=0, backupCount=0, ...); 'Rollover occurs whenever the current log file is nearly maxBytes in length; but if either of maxBytes or backupCount is zero, rollover never occurs, so you generally want to set backupCount to at least 1, and have a non-zero maxBytes.' WatchedFileHandler 'watches the file to see if it has changed since the last emit' for use with logrotate. Read through a summarizing fetch 2026-11-14 (page titled Python 3.15.2 documentation).

Relevant text: 'logging to a single file from multiple processes is not supported, because there is no standard way to serialize access to a single file across multiple processes in Python.' Read through a summarizing fetch 2026-11-14. invsync is one process, so a file handler that rotates is safe here.

Relevant text: if the name was the last link to a file but a process still has it open, 'the file will remain in existence until the last file descriptor referring to it is closed.' Read through a summarizing fetch 2026-11-14. That truncating the open file frees its blocks while the writer, which appends, carries on at the new end follows from the handler's default mode 'a'.

brief.situation: You support invsync, a Python service that syncs inventory between the warehouse system and the shop, on etl1 for Brightwater Garden Supply (fictional). Thursday's release went out with debug logging switched on. /var is 97% full and rising; PostgreSQL keeps its data on /var too and will stop when the disk is full, in about 12 minutes.
handover: invsync runs as one long-lived process under systemd; its logging is set up in /opt/invsync/invsync/logconf.py.
Nobody needs the debug lines, but keep at least the recent log if you can.
howItWorks: Run commands from the command line: type one, or pick it from the suggestions or the action list. Only this lab's commands run; there is no free shell, and each command's arguments are fixed.
Each command takes operator time: run it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. The outage keeps developing on the same clock.
The map shows each host, disk or service and the links between them, with a status in words. Output appears in the terminal as it happens.
When you declare the service restored, you write the incident record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the incident record: what filled /var, how you freed space without losing the service, and why the log will not do it again.

parts.label: Cause
parts.criteria: Names invsync's log: a plain FileHandler (never rotates) at DEBUG since Thursday's release.
parts.modelAnswer: du showed sync.log at 14 GB; logconf.py used logging.FileHandler with the root level at DEBUG.

parts.label: Freeing space
parts.criteria: Truncates the open file (or restarts after a delete) and explains that deleting a file a process holds open frees nothing until it closes.
parts.modelAnswer: truncate -s 0 freed the 14 GB at once while invsync kept appending; rm would have left the space held by the open descriptor until a restart.

parts.label: Lasting fix
parts.criteria: RotatingFileHandler (or TimedRotatingFileHandler) with a non-zero maxBytes and backupCount of at least 1, level INFO, restarted, and checked; explains why backupCount=0 never rolls over.
parts.modelAnswer: RotatingFileHandler(maxBytes=50 MB, backupCount=5) at INFO, restarted, and ls showed sync.log.1 after rollover. With backupCount at its default 0, rollover never occurs.

expertPath.text: df -h /var (97%) and du on /var/log/invsync: sync.log is 14 GB.
truncate -s 0 the open log: the space comes back at once and invsync keeps appending.
grep logconf.py: FileHandler at DEBUG. Switch to RotatingFileHandler(maxBytes=50 MB, backupCount=5) at INFO.
systemctl restart invsync; ls shows sync.log.1 after the first rollover.

fixed.headline: Good: space back, log bounded
fixed.body: You found the log, freed its space without deleting what the process still held, and bounded it with a handler that really rotates.

fixedGaps.headline: Space back, with gaps
fixedGaps.body: /var has room. The criteria show the gap: a plain FileHandler, or backupCount 0, refills the disk in about two hours.

dbStopped.headline: The database stopped
dbStopped.body: Deleting the file did not free the space: invsync still had it open. truncate frees it at once.

stillFilling.headline: Closed too soon
stillFilling.body: Check df after the fix: a deleted file held open still counts as used.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: du names the log. It is open in a long-lived process, so rm frees nothing (unlink keeps it until the last descriptor closes); truncate frees it now. Then fix the code: RotatingFileHandler with maxBytes and backupCount both non-zero (either at zero means no rollover) at INFO, restart to load it, and check that a .1 file appears.
